The skill: recognising vague language

Spoken English is full of deliberately imprecise expressions. There are two jobs they do.

  • When you cannot find the exact word: kind of, sort of. — It’s kind of reddish.
  • When there are more examples you are not going to list: and so on, and that kind / sort / type of thing, or whatever, and things / stuff / places like that. — The shop sells vintage clothes, records and that kind of thing.

Because these phrases are so common, they are said very fast and parts of the words disappear: kind of becomes something like kinda, sort of like sorta, like that like li'that, and so on like 'n so on. Recognising them matters more than producing them: if you hear them as noise, you lose the sentence around them.

1 · Read the explanation.
Building compound adjectives

What they are. Two words joined, usually by a hyphen, working together as one adjective: thick-rimmed, home-made, second-hand. English builds them freely, which is why you meet ones that are in no dictionary.

The common patterns. Adjective + past participle (clean-shaven, little-known); adverb + past participle (well-educated); adjective + present participle (tight-fitting, long-lasting); noun + past participle (home-made, hand-written); noun + noun (fixed-wheel, retro-style).

Never plural. Whatever the meaning, the compound does not change: thick-rimmed glasses (two rims), a six-month delay (six months), a two-hour film. The plural sits on the noun that follows.

Hyphen or not. Before a noun, hyphenate: a well-known band. After the verb, usually no hyphen: the band is well known. After an -ly adverb, never hyphenate: a brightly coloured dress, because -ly already shows the words belong together.

Order. The compound counts as one adjective and takes one slot in the sequence from lesson 41: a large black fixed-wheel bike.

When you cannot remember one. Use the vague language from this lesson: a sort of one-gear bike, the kind of glasses with thick frames. It is normal, it is fast, and it keeps the sentence moving.

The commonest errors at this level
  • thick-rimmeds glasses or a six-months delay — never plural.
  • a brightly-coloured dress — no hyphen after -ly.
  • hand-second — the order inside the compound is fixed.
  • tight fitting jeans before a noun — the hyphen is needed.
  • renowned of — it is renowned for.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Building one from scratch

What you want to say: a shirt with a pattern of checks, bought from a shop selling old clothes, that somebody has owned before.

Step 1 — find the compounds. A pattern of checks → checked or check-patterned. Old clothes shop → vintage. Owned before → second-hand.

Step 2 — freeze them. No plurals inside: not checks-patterned, not second-hands.

Step 3 — order them. Each compound takes one slot: opinion, then age, then type. a lovely second-hand check-patterned shirt — and three is the maximum before the noun.

Step 4 — if a word will not come. Hedge and keep going: a sort of checked shirt, second-hand, from a vintage place.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Six patterns, one hyphen

adjective + past participle is the commonest: clean-shaven, thick-rimmed, old-fashioned, little-known. adverb + past participle: well-educated, highly paid. adjective + present participle describes what the thing does: tight-fitting, good-looking, long-lasting. noun + past participle says how or where it was made: home-made, hand-written, sun-dried. noun + noun names a feature: fixed-wheel, retro-style, mid-century. number + noun: a two-hour film, a six-month delay — and the noun is always singular: a six-months delay.

When the hyphen disappears

Two rules cover almost every case. First, the hyphen belongs to the compound before a noun and is usually dropped after the verb: a well-known band against the band is well known. Second, an adverb ending in -ly takes no hyphen at all, in either position: a brightly coloured dress, a highly paid consultant — because -ly already shows that the adverb attaches to what follows.

A compound adjective sits in the adjective order from lesson 41 like any other adjective, in the slot its meaning belongs to: a large black fixed-wheel bike — size, colour, then the type.

And the participle inside a compound never takes a plural or a tense of its own: thick-rimmeds glasses, a hand-wrote note. Whatever else changes, the compound stays as it is.

Errors to watch: a six-months delay → six-month · a brightly-coloured dress → no hyphen after -ly · the band is well-known → usually well known after the verb · a hand-wrote note → hand-written.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

A group described from the inside

Anybody can list what a subculture wears. The harder task is saying what it is actually against.

The brief

Choose a group you have belonged to or watched closely — a subculture, a profession, a fan community, a neighbourhood. Describe how you would recognise a member, what they own, and what they reject. Then say what the description misses.

1 · Make notes before you speak. One line each.
1The group, and your relation to it:
2How you would recognise one, in three compounds:
3What they own that gives them away:
4What they reject, and why:
5What a description like yours always misses:
2 · Take the two roles, then swap.
Useful language
  • They tend to… · You rarely see a…
  • Clothes, music and that kind of thing.
  • It is all second-hand, or made to look…
  • What the description misses is…
Partner AYou · describing
  • Start with how you would recognise one.
  • Use compounds, and hedge when a word will not come.
  • Say what the group is against, not only what it wears.
  • End with what your own description leaves out.
Partner BYour teacher · the sceptic
  • Ask whether members would accept the label.
  • Challenge any detail that is only a stereotype.
  • Ask what the group has in common with the one before it.
  • Count the compound adjectives and the vague phrases.

Work in pairs. Five minutes. Then swap roles with a different group.Five minutes with your teacher, then swap roles with a different group.

Afterwards: name the part of your partner’s description that was a stereotype.

1 · Read the model.
Model · four paragraphs

You would know one from the shoes. Everything else about the climbing crowd at our local wall is deliberately ordinary — loose trousers, a plain T-shirt, nothing branded if they can help it — but the shoes are tight-fitting to the point of pain, brightly coloured, and usually second-hand from somebody two sizes down. Nobody who is serious buys new ones.

The equipment tells you more than the clothes. It is a low-tech crowd in a high-tech city: chalk bags that somebody’s mother sewed, home-made finger-training boards, hand-written notebooks of routes going back years. There are three or four people with expensive watches and everyone else treats them, kindly, as tourists. They mend things. A worn rope becomes a dog lead and then, eventually, something else.

What they are against is harder to say and it is the real thing. They are suspicious of anything that turns climbing into a product: competitions, sponsorship, gyms with branded lighting, obscure grading systems that only make sense on a screen. They talk about little-known crags the way other people talk about restaurants, and they genuinely do not want the crags to become renowned. The word they use for the mainstream version is “plastic”, which is unfair, and they know it is unfair, and they keep saying it.

What this description misses is that most of them would object to being described at all. If I had asked permission to write it, I would have got four different accounts and one flat refusal, and the refusal would have been the most accurate of the five.
